title: Baron's cabaret, Bricktop, Al Jolson and a ten-thousand-dollar bill
summary: Wooding recalls Bricktop as hostess at the whites-only Baron's, Leroy's whites-barred place, gangsters and a ten thousand dollar tip.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: Were you playing arrangements at this time?
Yes. I started playing arrangements. A funny thing happened to us there. Well, now we were in Baron's,
that's where I met and we become very good friends, with Bricktop.

Bricktop worked there, but later Snow worked with me. But Bricktop was the ruling singer. And they had a man there called Tony Donovan. Well, Tony was good because -- but Bricktop was the queen of the thing. Because Bricktop couldn't sing anything either. But she was a very fine hostess.

You know, and she made more money when you know you'd go from table to table. She made more money than anybody because I don't know -- she had a very pleasing disposition. Because we never had no colored people there, you know.

It was all white. And it was a funny thing. There was two brothers. Baron and Leroy. Baron Wilkins never had never allowed any of the colored people to come into his place. And Leroy never allowed any white people. But Leroy, -- one white man used to come into his place.

Yeah. Al Jolson was the only white man he that had a card to come in there. And nobody stopped him. But, Baron had a lot of the boys around there, a lot of the sportsmen around there, used to come upstairs and playing

and gambling and like that. But, because they sharped the white women, they wouldn't have them down there because the white women were the girl friends and the wives of the gangsters. And the beer barons was going at that time, you see?

I know that one time Bricktop was singing a piece on the floor, and that's about the only time I ever seen it. And a guy come up and said, 'Here Sam, sounds good.' And he handed me something, and it was just by chance, I happened to look at it. It was a ten thousand dollar bill. He had given one to the waiter too. You know, he was going to take them back, you know. We knew we wasn't going nowhere with it.
Over his dead body. But that was the first time I'd ever seen -- I believe it was the last time I've ever seen a ten thousand dollar bill.
But they loved the band, we played dances for them, we had a wonderful time there, see. And we stayed there for quite awhile, til I added another man. So there was seven.
